strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: the 'vision shortcut' / 'Information Collapse' pathology in VLA training, where language instructions become redundant given goal-driven dataset bias. The three pilot experiments (ID testing, ambiguous LIBERO Goal subset dropping to 12.4%, and near-0% OOD success) provide convincing empirical validation of the phenomenon.

The Bayesian decomposition framing (vision-only prior p(a|v) vs. language-conditioned posterior π(a|v,ℓ)) and the PMI/LLR objective is a clean and original lens on a practical failure mode, and the Appendix A derivation connecting the LLR to conditional PMI is correct.

The Latent Action Query mechanism is an elegant design: causal masking position controls information flow into the queries, enabling dual-branch training with a single shared VLM while incurring zero inference overhead.

Results are strong and multi-benchmark: +11.3% over the directly comparable QwenGR00T baseline on SimplerEnv (66.5% vs 55.2%, 480 trials/task) and a state-of-the-art 50.4% average on RoboCasa, beating Isaac-GR00T-N1.6 and OpenVLA-OFT.

The ablation (Table 3) properly separates the architectural contribution of action queries (+2.3%) from the Bayesian objective (+6.0%), supporting the central claim that the objective, not just the bottleneck architecture, drives gains.

The evaluation of general-capability preservation (Figs. 4-5) is a valuable addition often missing in VLA papers, and the honest discussion that vision-language (not just text-only) abilities may still degrade is commendable.
weaknesses: There is a conceptual gap between the theoretical objective and the practical loss. Eq. 4 motivates maximizing log π(a|v,ℓ)/p(a|v), but Eq. 7 instead maximizes log p(ℓ|v, H_Q^prior) − sg(log p(ℓ|v)). The paper itself is hand-wavy here ('we can compute a baseline p(ℓ|v) by detaching gradients or using a separate pass. However, a more direct and numerically stable approach is...'), so the actually-optimized objective is a variant whose equivalence to the stated PMI objective is not established. Additionally, Eq. 3 shows I(ℓ;a|v) ≤ H(ℓ|v) ≈ 0 under the very dataset bias being targeted, so the theoretical story of 'maximizing PMI' being possible on biased data is not fully resolved; gains may partly stem from regularization effects rather than the Bayesian narrative.

The experimental scope does not match the text. Section 4 promises results on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2', but only SimplerEnv and RoboCasa results are reported; no LIBERO or RoboTwin2 results appear, and real-robot experiments are absent ('currently underway').

The ablation study average (63.5% in Table 3) differs from the main SimplerEnv result (66.5% in Table 1) for the same BayesianVLA configuration without explanation, raising questions about run-to-run variance that is never quantified (no std/error bars or significance tests despite 480 trials).

No ablation of the two key hyperparameters λ and β, nor of the number of queries K, even though these directly control the objective trade-off central to the method. The complexity claim O(N²)→O(K²) for the DiT is asserted but not measured.

Gains on RoboCasa are more modest and uneven (50.4% vs 48.8% for OpenVLA-OFT), with BayesianVLA underperforming the baseline on several tasks (e.g., PnP Potato, Cuttingboard-to-Pot, Plate-to-Bowl), which deserves analysis.

The claimed marginal training overhead of the dual-branch setup is argued qualitatively but never quantified (no wall-clock or FLOP comparison), and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a method with nontrivial implementation choices (branch ordering, masking, stop-gradient placement).
